[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday reading: a program is read like a text or a list of wishes that the computer takes in all at once, so line order, goals of later lines or what the writer meant can matter. Java rule: each statement is one step, ended by ;, executed once, in written order, using only the current state.
[1] misconception (M) -> ComputerFillsInIntent: wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> ComputerFillsInIntent: Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
[3] misconception (M) -> StatementsRunInAnyOrder: wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.
[4] misconception (M) -> WhitespaceIsSignificant: wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.
[5] misconception (M) -> ProgramLooksAhead: wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

[0] names_the_element (N): A statement is one step of a program (a declaration, assignment, method call such as System.out.println(...), or control statement), ended by a semicolon when it is a simple statement.
[1] states_the_rule (S): A method body is a sequence of statements enclosed in braces and each followed by a semicolon; statements are executed for their effect and have no value; an expression statement evaluates its expression and discards any value.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Statements run one at a time, from first to last; each completes (normally or abruptly) before the next starts.
[1] output_prediction (OP): A statement has no value; its result is its effect: a changed variable, printed output, or a change of control flow.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Executing one statement applies its single effect to the current state (e.g. prints one string, or stores one value) and then control moves to the next statement.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Statements live in main's body; running the program executes main's statements in order.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): A block groups a sequence of statements in braces; the body of main() is such a block.
[2] relation_to_neighbour (R): System.out.print(s); is a statement, so its output appears exactly at its place in the sequence, with no newline.
[3] relation_to_neighbour (R): System.out.println(s); is a statement, so its line of output appears at its place in the sequence; swapping two println statements swaps the output lines.
[4] relation_to_neighbour (R): Control flow is the order in which statements run; without control statements it is straight-line, each once in order.
[5] relation_to_neighbour (R): A lone ; is the empty statement, which does nothing; it can fill a for-loop part or, by accident, end an if or loop header.
[6] relation_to_neighbour (R): An algorithm becomes a program as a sequence of statements, executed once each in the order given.
[7] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: a statement is the unit of action; a program is characterized by its sequence of statements, each doing one step of the algorithm.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> ComputerFillsInIntent: Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.
[1] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Each simple statement must end with ;. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: omitting the ; at the end of a statement: javac reports ';' expected (often at the end of that line or the next)
[2] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Write one statement per step and order them as the algorithm requires; straight-line sequence suffices when every step runs once, otherwise use conditionals or loops.
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: A ; directly after an if/while/for header is an empty statement. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: if (x > 0); or while (cond); followed by the intended body

Statements are written in main's body, and running the program executes main's statements in order, one by one.
An algorithm becomes a program as a sequence of statements, executed once each in the order given.
A statement block is a sequence of statements, each terminated by a semicolon, enclosed in braces; the body of main() is such a sequence.
Control flow is the order in which statements run.
Any part of a for loop, including its body, can be left empty (a null statement, a lone ;); the book prefers a while loop to null statements.
System.out.print(s); is itself a statement, so it runs at its own place in the sequence of statements.
System.out.println(s); is itself a statement, so its line of output appears at its own place in the sequence.
